purpose: Compare the Philippine primary diet evidence already reviewed for dalag (Channa striata) and Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus), and specify how Bangwit can present it without implying a fixed nationwide diet or bait advice.

studyEvidence.sampling: 180 wild fish collected in 2019 in selected municipalities around the lake, using gillnets; stomach contents were grouped and examined under microscopy.
contextAndLimits: Shrimp was the study's reported leading IRI food category in both seasonal groups; the results were pooled across municipalities and do not provide a locality-specific diet profile.
Fish remains were not identified to species and do not establish cannibalism.
The article's wet-season shrimp value differs between prose and table, and its listed IRI values do not normalize to 100; do not reuse the disputed percentages.
The journal policy states CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 but also has conflicting author-remix language; no adaptation or public-app reuse is approved.

studyEvidence.sampling: The article's Table 1 lists 11 Channa striata stomachs; collection dates and vouchers are not reported. Fish were obtained from local fishers and examined microscopically.
contextAndLimits: The paper reports algae in all examined Channa stomachs and insects in 30%; it does not list fish prey for this species in the Lake Wood sample.
The abstract says 144 stomachs were examined, while the nine species-level counts in Table 1 sum to 87; the discrepancy is unresolved.
This sample does not show that Channa striata never eats fish.
The article states CC BY-NC 4.0; product-level reuse remains unapproved.

studyEvidence.taxon: Channa striata (results table/conclusion; abstract typo: Channa strita)
studyEvidence.waterbody: Pampanga River, three unnamed sites in Cabiao, Nueva Ecija
studyEvidence.sampling: May 2019; 55 fish across six reported taxa; the paper gives no Channa-specific sample count or named/located station.
contextAndLimits: Whole prey is reported at Site 3 only; the prey is not identified, so this does not establish conspecific predation.
The paper uses a source spelling error and reports no voucher or independent specimen confirmation.
No item-level reuse license was verified; publication approval remains false.

studyEvidence.sampling: The article's Table 1 lists 7 Nile tilapia stomachs; collection dates and vouchers are not reported.
contextAndLimits: The authors describe opportunistic piscivory in this Lake Wood sample; the fish remains were not identified as tilapia or any other particular species.
The abstract/Table 1 sample-count conflict applies to this study; do not infer a national or fixed species diet from seven listed stomachs.
Do not transfer insect/shrimp findings for the unresolved Oreochromis sp. to O. niloticus.
The article states CC BY-NC 4.0; product-level reuse remains unapproved.

studyEvidence.sampling: Project report describes standardized gut analysis during a project spanning September 2011-August 2012, but the tilapia gut-sample count/date are unresolved and broader report dates conflict.
contextAndLimits: Cyanobacteria ranked highest in the report's pooled volumetric and importance measures. Sand is recorded as ingested material, not nutritional food.
The report says no predation on native fishes was observed in this sample; this is not a species-wide absence claim.
Exact sample size/date and item-specific reuse terms remain unresolved; no public-app diet row is approved.

studyEvidence.waterbody: Pampanga River, three unnamed sites in Cabiao, Nueva Ecija
studyEvidence.sampling: May 2019; 55 fish across six reported taxa; no Nile tilapia-specific sample count is stated.
contextAndLimits: The paper reports this taxon at Sites 1 and 3; no food-item-to-site crosswalk is supplied.
No species-specific sample count, voucher or item-level reuse license was verified.

crossStudyFindings.channaStriata: Philippine gut-content studies report shrimp and unidentified fish remains at Lake Mainit, whole prey of unspecified identity in one Cabiao site-level observation, and algae plus insects in the limited Lake Wood sample. These findings support context-specific dietary flexibility; none identifies Channa striata as the prey, so cannibalism is not established by the reviewed studies.
crossStudyFindings.oreochromisNiloticus: The reviewed Lake Manguao and Cabiao records emphasize cyanobacteria/algae, plant particles and phytoplankton in those study contexts. A small Lake Wood sample also reports fish remains, so a strict herbivore-only label is not supported. The reviewed species-specific sources do not establish worms or insects as a general Nile tilapia diet item; insect and shrimp results for an unresolved Oreochromis sp. must stay with that taxon label.
crossStudyFindings.comparisonLimit: The studies use different waterbodies, dates, sample sizes, methods and food-category resolution. Their metrics are not pooled or directly compared. A missing item in one sample is not proof that the fish never eats it elsewhere.

showPerRecord: sample count and size context when reported
productGuidance.tilapiaNameRule: Do not map an unqualified local name 'tilapia' to Oreochromis niloticus when the source reports Oreochromis sp. or does not identify species.

decision.reason: These records are useful answers to the example question, but they are historical site-specific studies with unresolved limitations and rights. Their findings cannot be presented as fixed nationwide diets or bait recommendations; none of the reviewed Dalag sources identifies conspecific prey.

nextAction: Continue the region-by-region inland and coastal source sweep. Keep existing research summaries separate from the app projection; obtain item-specific reuse review/permission where necessary before designing public diet cards, and preserve species, waterbody, method, period, sample-size and uncertainty context in any future record.
